opus-5.5.text:
I think what they're doing is genuinely impressive, and I don't want to dismiss it. Genie, Runway, Luma: the visual quality, the temporal consistency, and in Genie's case the interactivity, where you press a key and the world responds. A few years ago that would have seemed like science fiction. So as engineering and as a product direction, I have a lot of respect for it.

But I think we need to be careful about what we mean by "world model." A lot of the current approach starts from video generation. The objective is to produce pixels that look right to a human viewer. That's a very natural objective if you're building a creative tool, or a game engine, or something for entertainment. It's less clear to me that it's the right objective if what you want is a system that actually *understands* the world, one that can reason, plan, and predict the consequences of actions.

The core issue is that pixels are an extremely redundant, high-dimensional signal, and most of that information is irrelevant for decision-making. If I'm planning to pick up a cup, I don't need to predict the exact texture of the tablecloth or how the light reflects off the wall. A generative model trained to reconstruct pixels has to spend enormous capacity on those details. And it can get the surface statistics right while the underlying physics or causal structure is wrong. We've all seen videos where objects merge or appear out of nowhere, but each frame still looks beautiful. That's a sign the model is optimizing for appearance, not for a model of the world.

So my view is that generation and understanding are related, but they're not the same thing. Being able to render something doesn't mean you have a good internal representation of it. I'm more interested in world models that predict in a learned representation space, an abstract latent space, rather than in pixel space. The model learns what matters and discards what doesn't, and then you plan in that space. Generation can still be useful, as a decoder, for visualization, for humans to inspect what the model "imagines." But it shouldn't be the foundation.

There's also a practical point. A lot of the generative approach is built on the premise that scale will solve everything: more video data, bigger models, more compute, and understanding will emerge. Maybe some of it will. But I think we've learned from language models that scaling a next-token objective gets you very far and also leaves real gaps in grounding, physical reasoning, and planning. I'd rather think carefully about the objective and the representation now than assume scaling will fix it later.

That said, I don't see it as either-or. These companies are pushing on data pipelines, on infrastructure, on how to handle long video, on interactivity, and all of that is valuable to the whole field. And the products can be very successful even if they aren't the path to general intelligence. I just think that for the deeper goal of an AI that understands the physical world the way animals and humans do, we need something beyond making good-looking video.

r001.rationale: The response describes their approach as starting from video generation and notes Genie’s interactivity, but it does not characterize the companies as primarily building simulators for world models despite their positioning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually important to distinguish between two things that often get lumped together under the term "world model." One is the generative video approach, which is what Genie, Runway, Luma, and also Sora are pursuing. The other is what I'd call representation-first world modeling, which is closer to what Yann LeCun has been advocating with JEPA, and honestly closer to where my own thinking has drifted.

The generative approach has an obvious appeal. You take enormous amounts of video, you train a model to predict the next frame or to reconstruct the frames in pixel space, and you get something that looks like it understands physics. Objects fall, liquids pour, shadows move. And for a product like Runway or Luma, that's the whole point. The output is the product. A filmmaker wants beautiful, controllable pixels, and whether the model has an internal notion of gravity is almost irrelevant as long as the water looks right.

Genie is a bit different and I find it more interesting from a research standpoint, because it's interactive. You give it actions and it rolls the world forward. That's conceptually closer to what a world model is supposed to do: predict the consequences of actions. But it's still fundamentally generating pixels, and that's where my hesitation comes in.

My concern is that pixel reconstruction is a very expensive and somewhat misleading training signal. Most of the bits in a video are irrelevant to planning or reasoning. The exact texture of leaves moving in the wind, the precise noise pattern on a wall, these consume a huge fraction of model capacity, and the model is rewarded for getting them right. Meanwhile the things that actually matter for an agent, like where the object will be in two seconds, whether this surface is traversable, what happens if I push this, are a tiny fraction of the information and can get buried. We saw a version of this in our own work on diffusion models with REPA, where aligning intermediate features to a strong pretrained visual representation sped up training dramatically. That told me the generation itself wasn't learning good representations very efficiently. The representation was the bottleneck, not the decoder.

So the way I see it, the generative companies are building an incredibly impressive rendering engine, and sometimes a decent simulator, and they're calling it a world model. There's nothing wrong with that commercially. But if the goal is a model that an agent, a robot, or a reasoning system can actually use to think, I believe the prediction should happen in representation space, not pixel space. You predict abstract states, you measure error in that latent space, and you only decode to pixels when a human needs to look at it.

There's also the question of whether scale alone closes the gap. The optimistic view, which I think many of these companies hold, is that with enough video and enough compute, a good internal world model emerges as a byproduct of generation, the way language models seemed to pick up reasoning as a byproduct of next-token prediction. I'm honestly not sure the analogy holds. Language is already a compressed, human-abstracted representation. Video is raw sensory data. The compression work that language had done for us still has to be done by the model, and I don't think forcing it to decompress back to pixels is the right way to learn that compression.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive. The engineering in these systems is remarkable, the data pipelines are real contributions, and the fact that they're interactive and controllable means they'll generate a lot of useful signal for the field. I just think of them as one path among several, and probably not the one that gets us to a genuine world model for intelligence. I'd expect the eventual winner to combine strong self-supervised representation learning with a generative component that's used sparingly, mostly for visualization and for grounding, rather than as the core learning objective.

r001.rationale: The response describes Runway and Luma mainly as pixel-generating products and calls them rendering engines that are only sometimes decent simulators. It does not characterize these companies as primarily building simulators for world models.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but the key question is what we mean by a world model. If we mean a model that can generate a plausible continuation of a video, that’s one thing. If we mean a model that understands how the world changes when you take an action, and can support planning, that’s a stronger requirement.

Video generation gives you a very rich learning signal. To predict what happens next, a model has to capture something about motion, objects, and their interactions. So I wouldn’t dismiss that approach. The question is how much of what it learns is reliable enough to use beyond generating convincing images.

For example, a video can look realistic while getting an interaction wrong. For a viewer, that might be a small artifact. For an agent using the model to decide what to do, it could be the whole problem. You want to ask: Can I intervene? Does the model respond consistently to different actions? Does it preserve the state of the world over time?

So I see generation as an important ingredient. But I’d evaluate a world model by whether it helps a system predict, plan, and act—not just by how impressive the generated video looks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses video generation as a possible ingredient in world models, but does not say Genie, Runway, and Luma are primarily building simulators or contrast that with their positioning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising direction. But I would separate two questions: can a model generate a video that looks plausible, and can it predict how the world changes when you take an action? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

For me, the interesting part of a world model is that you can interact with it. If I take a different action, does the outcome change in a consistent way? Does the model preserve what’s happening in the scene over time, including things that are temporarily out of view? A beautiful video alone doesn’t tell us that.

So I’m excited about these approaches, but I wouldn’t judge them only by visual quality. I’d want to see whether an agent can use the model to plan, make decisions, and then have those decisions work outside the generated environment. That’s a much stronger test of whether the model has learned something useful about the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating world models by interaction and action-conditioned prediction, but it does not characterize Genie, Runway, and Luma as primarily building simulators or contrast that with their positioning.
